rationale: mutation_score=0.667 is below the 0.5 threshold's safe margin conceptually but the real disqualifier is validation_status=fail with two uncovered_requirement issues (FR4, SR1) confirmed by the analyzer as genuine detection gaps, not defective mutants. Examining the SR1 mutant: it changes duty_plus2 from duty+2 to duty+1, which genuinely narrows the dead-time gap and should cause pwm_hi/pwm_lo overlap for some duty/en sequences -- this is a real, observable violation of SR1's no-overlap invariant. Yet SR1 passed against this mutant (0/1 detected), meaning the SR1 check in tb_top.v is not actually exercising a duty/timing region where the induced overlap becomes observable, or its randomized en toggling + duty sweep does not hit the boundary case the mutant corrupts. Similarly the FR4 mutant removes the explicit hold branch for cnt when en=0, which under Verilog's if/else-if semantics falls through to no assignment when rst=0 and en=0 -- this genuinely could change simulation behavior (retains previous value via implicit non-blocking assignment absence, which in iverilog behaves as an implicit latch/hold at the signal level, but timing subtleties around when duty changes during the hold could produce observable divergence). Analyzer confirms FR4's scenario window may be too narrow to isolate hold-specific mismatches from other simultaneous FR failures. Both mutants are legitimate corruptions of real requirements per their expected_detection rationale; the checks themselves are insufficiently discriminating. This is an evaluation_framework defect, not a mutant defect.
revision_instructions: Two requirement checks in the evaluation harness (evaluation/tb_top.v and evaluate.py) fail to detect genuine corruptions of the behavior they are supposed to guard, per mutation testing. Fix both: (1) SR1 (no-overlap invariant): the current check sweeps duty=0..15 with randomized en toggling over >=3 periods and asserts pwm_hi & pwm_lo == 0 every cycle, but it did not catch a submission where the required two-cycle dead-time gap after the duty boundary was narrowed to one cycle (i.e. the low-side window begins one cycle earlier than the pinned interface's duty+2 offset requires). Strengthen the SR1 check so it exercises boundary-region duty values deterministically (not only randomly) -- specifically ensure duty values where a one-cycle-early low-side window would abut the tail of the high-side window are included in every run, and increase the assertion window so any single-cycle overlap during the boundary transition is guaranteed to be sampled and reported as a failure, regardless of random seed. Also add or tighten the SR2 dead-time-width check to independently catch narrowed gaps, since a width violation should also fail SR2 discriminatively. (2) FR4 (enable-hold behavior): the current check compares cycle-by-cycle output against the reference during an en=0 hold of at least 8 cycles and after resuming, but it did not catch a submission whose internal free-running counter update logic omits the explicit hold-on-disable branch, potentially causing incorrect counter retention or drift during the held interval. Isolate the FR4 scenario so it is not confounded by simultaneous FR1-FR3 failures: run a dedicated test that (a) holds en=0 for at least 8 cycles starting from several different counter/duty phase offsets (not just one fixed phase), (b) checks that the counter's held value is externally observable as unchanging via the pwm_hi/pwm_lo outputs matching the reference exactly on every one of those held cycles, and (c) checks correct resumption behavior (counter continues from the held value, not from a corrupted value) for at least 4 cycles after re-enabling. Both checks must grade purely through simulated output behavior of the compiled submission against the reference waveform -- never by inspecting submission source structure -- so any correct rewrite of the counter/comparator logic that satisfies the pinned interface passes, while a submission with a narrowed dead-time gap or a broken hold-on-disable path fails.'
